notes: V5 Stage 3 (Issue #16) source registry. Deliberately a small, real, independently verified seed set spanning the requested domains (A: weight vs fat loss, B: fasting, C: GLP-1/semaglutide, D: tirzepatide, E: protein/lean mass, F: hydration, G: weight regulation/adaptive thermogenesis) — not a bulk-generated corpus. Every record's verification block reflects an actual check performed against the cited URL/identifier during Stage 3 (PubMed for journal articles, DailyMed for FDA drug labels, nationalacademies.org for the DRI report), not an assertion made from memory. A small high-quality seed is intentional; Issue #17 will grow this registry as real article research occurs.

sources.title: Beyond body mass index
sources.notes: Exact publication day within August 2001 not shown on the PubMed record; day-of-month defaulted to the 1st. Core point: BMI is only a surrogate measure of body fatness, not a direct measurement.

verification.verification_method: Direct WebFetch of the PubMed abstract page; confirmed title, authors, journal, year, volume/issue, DOI, and PMID against the record.

sources.title: Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Health, Aging, and Disease
sources.notes: Authors affiliated with NIA/NIH (de Cabo) and Johns Hopkins (Mattson). A narrative review, not a primary trial — cited only for definitional/mechanistic overview claims, not for a specific numeric efficacy result. Status changed from "current" to "corrected" during the Stage 3 closure pass (Issue #28) after independently confirming this article carries two published NEJM errata (see corrections[] below) — this is a factual correction to the source record, not a downgrade in how much the claim citing it can be trusted; see lib/evidence-support-policy.ts for why "corrected" still counts as active support.

verification.verification_method: Direct WebFetch of the PubMed abstract page; confirmed title, authors, journal, exact date, volume/pages, DOI, and PMID against the record.

corrections.description: NEJM erratum (N Engl J Med. 2020;382(3):298): in the second paragraph of the "Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Health and Aging" section (original page 2544), the final sentence should have begun "There was an inverse relationship between adiposity reduction and life span," rather than "...between adiposity and life span." Concerns the adiposity/lifespan association discussion, not the metabolic-switch mechanism section this registry's claim draws from.
corrections.notes: claim-fasting-metabolic-switch makes no statement about adiposity/lifespan association, so this correction does not affect it.

corrections.description: NEJM erratum (N Engl J Med. 2020;382(10):978): in the first paragraph of the "Intermittent Fasting and Metabolic Switching" section (original page 2542), the fifth sentence should have read that in humans, ketone-body blood levels rise within 8-12 hours after the onset of fasting, reaching 0.2-0.5 mM maintained through 24 hours, with a subsequent increase to 1-2 mM by 48 hours — rather than the original text's "reaching levels as high as 2 to 5 mM by 24 hours." References 15 and 16 were also replaced. This is in the same section (metabolic switching) that claim-fasting-metabolic-switch draws from.
corrections.notes: claim-fasting-metabolic-switch is a general statement that fasting shifts fuel use from glucose to ketones — it does not cite any specific ketone concentration (mM) value or specific hour threshold, so the corrected numbers do not touch anything this claim actually asserts. Independently re-confirmed via search of the erratum's described correction text before reaching this determination; not assumed.

sources.title: Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Adults with Overweight or Obesity
sources.notes: Epub 2021-02-10, print 2021-03-18; publication_date reflects the print/journal date. N=1,961. Mean weight change -14.9% semaglutide vs -2.4% placebo at week 68; treatment difference -12.4 percentage points (95% CI -13.4 to -11.5, P<0.001); >=5% weight loss in 86.4% (semaglutide) vs 31.5% (placebo).

verification.verification_method: Direct WebFetch of the PubMed abstract page; confirmed title, authors, journal, exact date, volume/pages, DOI, PMID, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registration number against the record.

sources.title: WEGOVY (semaglutide) injection and tablets — FDA-approved prescribing information
sources.publisher_or_journal: Novo Nordisk Pharmaceutical Industries, LP (FDA-approved labeling; distributed via NIH DailyMed)
sources.notes: Replaces the retired 2024 repackaged listing (see src-fda-wegovy-label-2024-repackaged-historical) during the Stage 3 closure pass (Issue #28). This is the current official Novo Nordisk manufacturer label (not a repackager listing), covering both the original once-weekly subcutaneous injection and a newer oral tablet formulation. The label's own footer states "Revised: 6/2026" (day-of-month not given there, defaulted to the 1st for publication_date); DailyMed's separate page metadata additionally shows "Updated June 18, 2026" for when this SPL version was posted to DailyMed — recorded here for transparency but not used as publication_date, since it describes DailyMed's posting rather than the label's own revision date. Materially expanded since the 2024 label: the injection formulation is now also approved for pediatric patients (12 years and older) with obesity, and for treatment of noncirrhotic MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) with moderate-to-advanced liver fibrosis (stages F2-F3) in adults; a new oral tablet formulation is approved for the same adult weight-management and cardiovascular-risk-reduction indications as the injection, but the tablet is NOT indicated for pediatric use or MASH per this label. Boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and the MTC/MEN2 contraindication were confirmed unchanged from the 2024 label.

verification.verification_method: Three separate direct WebFetch calls against the DailyMed HTML label page: (1) confirmed labeler (Novo Nordisk Pharmaceutical Industries, LP), drug name/active ingredient, and both formulations; (2) quoted the exact INDICATIONS AND USAGE text for each formulation; (3) quoted the label's own "Revised: 6/2026" line and DailyMed's separate page-metadata "Updated June 18, 2026" date.

sources.title: Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity
sources.notes: Epub 2022-06-04, print 2022-07-21; publication_date reflects the print/journal date. N=2,539. sources.title: Persistent metabolic adaptation 6 years after "The Biggest Loser" competition
sources.notes: Exact publication day within August 2016 not shown on the PubMed record; day-of-month defaulted to the 1st. Long-term (6-year) follow-up cohort, not an RCT. Key finding: measured resting metabolic rate at 6-year follow-up was 704 +/- 427 kcal/day below the same participants' measured baseline RMR, despite substantial weight regain in most participants. Separately, the paper's adjusted 'metabolic adaptation' residual (relative to predicted RMR after accounting for body composition and age) was -499 +/- 207 kcal/day — a distinct, smaller-magnitude figure never interchangeable with the raw measured-baseline comparison. (Corrected during a follow-up Issue #28 review pass: this note previously mischaracterized the -704 comparator as a "baseline-predicted value.")

verification.verification_method: Direct WebFetch of the PubMed abstract page; confirmed title, authors, journal, year/month, volume/pages, DOI, and PMID against the record.

sources.title: Daily energy expenditure through the human life course
sources.notes: Large cross-sectional doubly-labeled-water dataset (males and females aged 8 days to 95 years), not a longitudinal trial of any single individual across the lifespan. Added during the Stage 4 legacy corpus audit (Issue #17) to verify a specific statistical claim in the existing article 'understanding-your-metabolism-facts-vs-myths'. The abstract confirms fat-free-mass-adjusted energy expenditure 'remains stable in adulthood (20 to 60 years), even during pregnancy... then declines in older adults,' but the abstract itself does not state a specific per-year percentage decline rate after 60. The commonly cited 'approximately 0.7% per year' figure was corroborated via a secondary source (Healio news summary of the study) rather than a direct quote from the primary abstract text — recorded here as a limitation, not resolved by inventing a primary-source quote.

verification.verification_method: Direct WebFetch of the PubMed abstract page; confirmed title, authors, journal, volume/issue/pages, DOI, and PMID, and quoted the exact life-course energy-expenditure pattern. The specific 0.7%/year post-60 decline rate was additionally checked via a secondary WebSearch summary (Healio), since the PubMed abstract text itself does not state that number — this is disclosed, not treated as directly primary-verified.

sources.title: Dietary sugars intake and cardiovascular health: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association
sources.notes: Added during the Stage 4 legacy corpus audit (Issue #17) to verify the specific AHA added-sugar limit numbers repeated across several existing articles (e.g. 'no more than 25g/6 tsp for women, 36g/9 tsp for men'). The abstract states the recommendation in calories, not grams or teaspoons: no more than 100 calories/day (women) and 150 calories/day (men) from added sugars, representing half the discretionary calorie allowance under the 2005 Dietary Guidelines. The gram/teaspoon figures commonly quoted in consumer content are a conversion (roughly 4 kcal/g of sugar) of this calorie-based recommendation, not a separate primary figure — this is disclosed so a future rewrite cites the calorie basis accurately rather than treating grams as the AHA's own original unit. This is a 2009 statement; AHA has not been independently re-verified this session to have superseded these specific numbers with a more recent statement — flagged as a currentness item for a full rewrite pass, not resolved here.

verification.verification_method: Direct WebFetch of the PubMed abstract page; confirmed title, authors, journal, exact volume/issue/pages, DOI, PMID, and the exact calorie-based recommendation text (100 kcal/day women, 150 kcal/day men).
